newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel will keep much of West Bank in pullbacks - PM.
newsitem.headline: Israel will keep much of West Bank in pullbacks - PM.

text.p: Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said on Friday Israel would not give most of the West Bank to Palestinians in pullbacks under an interim period before a final peace deal.

He said his proposal to bypass three interim Israeli troop withdrawals from the West Bank to complete "final status" talks within six months, nearly two years earlier than planned, would remove the need to waste time haggling over the redeployments.

The Israeli leader vehemently denied a report by Israel's Maariv daily that, in a permanent peace deal, he would recognise a Palestinian state in half of the West Bank and remove some Jewish settlements.

"With these redeployments it is already clear on the side of the Palestinians that the idea that we'd give them each time 20 or 30 percent or a significant percentage...that is not realistic," Netanyahu told Israel Radio.
"That won't work with the government, not with my government," he said. "I propose going to another process."
The Palestinians rejected Netanyahu's proposal, revealed on Wednesday, as a trick to deflect world attention from Israel building a new Jewish settlement in Arab East Jerusalem.

Palestinians have also rejected Israel's unilateral decision that the first pullback would constitute only nine percent of West Bank land now under some Israeli control -- seven percent now under joint Israel-PLO control and only two percent that is under sole Israeli control.
Israel has handed over eight major West Bank towns and much of the Gaza Strip to Palestinian rule since signing a historic framework interim peace deal in 1993.

Netanyahu recommitted Israel to the further pullbacks, the last to be in mid-1998, in a deal signed under U.S. auspices in January. Final status peace talks did not resume on March 17 as had been agreed in the January deal after the unilateral Israeli decisions to build the Jewish settlement and on redeployment.
Netanyahu sent top aide Dore Gold to Egypt for talks with Osama el-Baz, President Hosni Mubarak's foreign policy adviser, on Thursday.

"His proposals are unconvincing," Egyptian Foreign Minister Amr Moussa told Reuters. "I am unable now to say what these proposals are but I would like to tell you all that any ideas they are talking about that try to justify or circumvent what's happening in Jerusalem is rejected."

Maariv said on Friday that Netanyahu would recognise a Palestinian state -- without an army -- in up to half of the West Bank. It said some Jewish settlements might be dismantled tp prevent them being "islands" in a Palestinian state.
It also said Netanyahu would allow flags other than Israel's to fly over non-Jewish holy sites in Jerusalem.
"I am against a Palestinian state...I have no intention and I am not taking down any settlement...I never said a thing or half a thing about flags," Netanyahu told the radio.
Maariv said Netanyahu had briefed Jordan's King Hussein on his "plan" for a final peace settlement with the Palestinians when the king visited Israel on Sunday.
It quoted Netanyahu as saying: "If the Palestinians insist on their demands, there will be no agreement."
Palestinians want to establish a state in all of the West Bank and Gaza Strip with Arab East Jerusalem as capital.
Israel captured the areas in the 1967 Middle East war. It annexed Arab East Jerusalem in a move not recognised internationally and says it will never cede any part of its "eternal" capital.
